# Summary: Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering American computer scientist, electrical engineer, inventor, and transgender activist. She made seminal contributions to computer architecture, notably inventing multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling while at IBM Research in the 1960s on the Advanced Computing Systems (ACS) project—work foundational to superscalar processor design. After transitioning gender in 1968 and facing discrimination including being fired by IBM, Conway rebuilt her career, contributing significantly to very-large-scale integration (VLSI) design methodology at Xerox PARC alongside Carver Mead. She co-authored the influential textbook *Introduction to VLSI Systems* , taught a landmark VLSI design course at MIT, and founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology and the MOSIS prototype system that greatly simplified chip fabrication and design, fueling the VLSI revolution.
Conway later worked at DARPA and served as a professor and associate dean at the University of Michigan before retiring as professor emerita in 1998. Throughout her career, she was recognized with numerous awards, including IEEE Fellow, IEEE/RSE James Clerk Maxwell Medal, membership in the National Academy of Engineering, and election to the Computer History Museum Hall of Fellows. In 2020, IBM publicly apologized for firing her and honored her with its Lifetime Achievement Award. Beyond technical innovation, Conway was a vocal transgender rights advocate, raising awareness, offering support through her website, and campaigning for inclusive ethics codes in engineering societies. She passed away in June 2024 at age 86, leaving a lasting legacy both as a trailblazing engineer and as a pioneer for transgender inclusion in STEM.
